I read the current default calibration of the real garnet (set f81c45da-6e73-4b5d-a0fe-72c75635fade) and compared every 3-qubit chain. The best one is QB11-QB12-QB7, with QB12 in the middle. Its two IRB CZ fidelities are 0.99869 (QB12-QB11) and 0.99802 (QB12-QB7), so the product is about 0.99671. The next best chains are lower: QB8 in the middle (QB13, QB3) gives 0.9936, and QB20 in the middle (QB19, QB16) gives 0.9934.

I then ran a 3-qubit GHZ circuit on garnet:mock with 200 shots. It puts a Hadamard on QB12, then CNOT from QB12 to QB11 and from QB12 to QB7, then measures all three. Each CNOT is built from one CZ plus single-qubit rotations. I read the payload back from the server and it has exactly 2 CZ gates, on QB12-QB11 and QB12-QB7, and measures QB11, QB12 and QB7. Job 01a160a6-86c9-7655-b4f3-37ea9d20e4f8 completed.

The counts were 000: 56, 111: 52, 001: 46 and 110: 46. Bit order is Qiskit style, with the rightmost bit being QB11, the middle bit QB12 and the leftmost QB7. A perfect GHZ state would give only 000 and 111. The mock returns counts that do not reflect the circuit, so these four outcomes are not a real result and say nothing about GHZ quality. The principle shown is that on a real chip you pick the qubits whose two-qubit gates have the lowest error, because errors multiply along the chain. The product of the two CZ fidelities (about 99.7 percent) is a rough upper bound on how well the entangling step works. Only a run on the real garnet, which I did not do, would show the true GHZ counts.
